title: Google Fonts adds Redaction for free; Gemini Notebook now shows its outline before it generates slides
dek: A legal-document serif goes free, AI tools add a review step, CSS gets a random() function, and two Config-week videos.
preheader: Redaction lands on Google Fonts, Gemini lets you edit the plan first, and CSS random() arrives in Chrome.
hero_alt: Rr, Gg and Qq in three typefaces with wave rules between
summary: Google is putting a checkpoint into AI generation: [Gemini Notebook now lets you review and edit the outline](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/products/gemini-notebook/co-create-slides-videos/) before it builds slides or a video, a pattern worth borrowing for any generative feature you design. On the craft side, [CSS random() has shipped in Safari and is rolling out in Chrome](https://www.smashingmagazine.com/2026/10/embracing-playful-imperfection-css-random-function/), so controlled imperfection no longer needs JavaScript. [Redaction, the serif MCKL drew from the type of American court papers](https://fonts.google.com/specimen/Redaction), is now free on Google Fonts with its six degraded cuts. And Apple's [Designers of Tomorrow showcase opened in Paris](https://9to5mac.com/2026/10/20/apples-designers-of-tomorrow-highlights-creative-projects-from-emerging-designers) with a jury that included its VP of industrial design.

typeface.name: Redaction
typeface.by: Jeremy Mickel, MCKL, with creative direction by Forest Young
typeface.pair: Set headlines in Redaction and keep UI and body text in a plain grotesque such as Inter, so the legal-document voice reads as intentional.
typeface.good_for: Editorial headlines, pull quotes, civic and justice-themed products
typeface.note: Commissioned for The Redaction, Titus Kaphar and Reginald Dwayne Betts's 2019 work at MoMA PS1, it heightens the Times New Roman and Century Schoolbook of court papers with soft round terminals and razor-thin strokes. Google Fonts added it this month along with Redaction 10 to 100, cuts that get progressively rougher, like a document photocopied too many times.

learn.title: A safe starter for CSS random()
learn.intro: Drop this into a prototype to give cards or tags a hand-placed wobble that only appears where the browser supports it and stays flat for people who ask for less motion.
learn.code_note: Keep the ranges tiny for anything people read or click. A by step snaps values to your spacing scale, and a shared key keeps squares square.
learn.take: The reduced-motion wrapper around rotation is our own caution; the article recommends flattening angles for those users.

learn.title: Controlled randomness in interfaces
learn.intro: CSS can now pick a value at random inside a range you set, so layouts can feel handmade without a script deciding every angle.
learn.define: random(min, max) returns a value between two bounds of the same unit, optionally snapped to a step with the by keyword, and a named key lets several properties share one result.

examples.name: Firefox
examples.text: Not shipped yet, so plan a fallback.

tips: Randomise decoration, never structure: tilt a sticker or a card shadow, but keep body text, grids and tap targets fixed.
Use a by step to snap random values to your spacing or rotation scale, so the mess still belongs to the system.
Pair random() with sibling-index() for a fan or stack that is ordered first and only lightly jittered second.
Wrap it in @supports with a static fallback, and flatten angles for people who prefer reduced motion.
Hide per-letter spans from screen readers if you jitter individual characters.
learn.why: Brand teams keep asking for warmth and imperfection; this gives you a way to spec it in tokens and ranges that engineers can ship without custom scripts.
